chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Volatility Smile and Skew

lessons.title: Trading and Risk Implications of a Steepening Skew

children.text: From Watching Skew to Trading Around It

Three lessons in, you can name the skew, measure its steepness, and read what it says about who is hedging. This closing lesson of the chapter is about what changes in how you actually trade and manage risk once you take skew seriously, instead of treating every strike as if it were priced off one shared, flat volatility.
Why "Selling the Skew" Is Not Free Money

Farhan's strangle in Lesson 2 already showed the core idea: the put side of an equity skew is structurally richer than the equidistant call side, and selling it collects more premium precisely because it carries more of the real crash risk the skew exists to price. Systematically selling OTM Nifty puts to harvest that richness is a real, popular strategy, run by everyone from retail theta-sellers to systematic funds. It can look extremely profitable for long stretches, because most weeks nothing dramatic happens and the premium is simply collected. That is also exactly the shape of risk finance people describe as picking up nickels in front of a steamroller: steady small gains, funded by a real, if infrequent, chance of a large loss that can erase years of them at once.

A related, more aggressive structure sometimes pitched as "harvesting the skew" even harder is the put ratio spread: buy one nearer-the-money put, and sell two or more further OTM puts against it, pocketing the extra premium from the richer, further-out short legs. This leaves the position net short an extra, uncovered put beneath the lower strike. In a genuinely large crash, exactly the scenario the skew has been pricing all along, that uncovered leg is what turns the premium you were harvesting into the loss that consumes it, and then some.

body.text: Skew being rich is not a pricing error waiting to be captured for free. It is compensation for a real, if infrequent, risk. Any strategy built around selling that richness needs position sizing and risk limits built for the tail event it is implicitly short, not just for the calm weeks that make up most of its track record.

children.text: Risk Reversals as a Trade, Not Just a Metric

Lesson 3 used the risk reversal (OTM put IV minus equidistant OTM call IV) purely as a way to measure skew steepness. It is also a tradeable structure in its own right: sell the richer OTM put, buy the cheaper OTM call, and you get directional upside exposure while the expensive put helps pay for it, rather than paying full price for a call outright.

body.caption: Illustrative bullish risk reversal on Nifty (Spot: 24,800, 30 days to monthly expiry)

children.text: Notice this position is not free of skew risk either. It is still net short a put on the exact strike that carries the market's crash pricing, so it is a bullish view expressed partly by taking on some of the same tail exposure Lesson 2's Farhan and this lesson's put-sellers carry, just alongside genuine long-call upside. A risk reversal trade is a deliberate, sized decision to be short skew in one direction, not a way to avoid the risk entirely.
Skew Is Not Static When Spot Moves: Sticky Strike vs Sticky Delta
Everything so far has looked at skew as a snapshot. The moment Nifty actually moves, the whole curve has to reshuffle, and desks describe two different conventions for how that reshuffling happens.

columns.label: Sticky Strike
points: Each strike keeps its own IV fixed even as spot moves
A specific rupee strike's IV stays pinned to what it was
The whole skew shape effectively shifts sideways with spot, since the ATM point now sits at a different strike
A simplifying assumption some risk systems use, but not a great match for how liquid index skew usually behaves

columns.label: Sticky Delta (Sticky Moneyness)
points: Each strike's IV is defined by its distance from the current ATM point, not its fixed rupee strike
As spot moves, the whole skew curve moves with it, keeping its shape relative to the new ATM
Closer to how Nifty and Bank Nifty skew typically behaves in ordinary market conditions
Still only an approximation: skew can steepen beyond a plain sticky-delta shift once a genuine crash is underway

children.text: That last line matters more than it looks. In a real, sharp selloff, skew does not just travel down with spot the way sticky delta alone would predict. It typically steepens further on top of that, because the exact institutional hedging demand from Lesson 3 accelerates precisely when the crash everyone was insuring against starts to look real.

body.caption: Vanna measures how much an option's delta shifts when volatility changes, equivalently how much its vega shifts when spot moves. It is the specific Greek governing how a skewed book's risk reshapes itself as the market moves, a topic beyond this course's current scope, but worth knowing by name once you are trading skew rather than just observing it.

children.text: Risk Management Takeaway: Stress-Test the Shape, Not Just the Level

A common shortcut in risk systems is to stress-test an options book by shifting every strike's IV up by the same flat amount, say 5 percentage points across the board, and re-pricing the portfolio from there. For a book with meaningful skew exposure, particularly one short OTM puts, this understates real risk, because it misses exactly the behavior the last section just described: in a genuine selloff, the lower strikes do not just rise by the same amount as everything else, they tend to rise by more, as the skew itself steepens. A risk manager who only shocks the level, and not the slope, of the skew is stress-testing a crash that has never actually happened this way in a liquid index market.

body.title: Reading a clean track record correctly
body.question: A systematic fund sells 1-month OTM Nifty puts every week to harvest the elevated skew-driven premium, and it has been profitable for two straight years in a calm, grinding bull market. What is the most important risk this track record does not yet reflect?
options: Nothing; a two-year profitable track record is sufficient proof the strategy is safe

The strategy has not yet been tested through a genuine sharp selloff, precisely the scenario the rich put IV it has been collecting exists to price; a single large crash can erase years of collected premium and more
Selling puts can never lose money as long as the fund remains disciplined about entry timing
Skew has no real connection to how profitable a systematic put-selling strategy turns out to be
body.explanation: A calm, rising market is precisely the environment where a skew-selling strategy looks best and is tested least. The rich premium it collects is compensation for a rare, large downside move, and a track record built entirely in calm conditions says almost nothing about how the strategy survives the exact event it is implicitly short.

body.title: A risk manager's flat stress test
body.scenario: A risk manager at a proprietary trading desk runs the firm's standard VaR model, which stress-tests the options book by shifting every strike's IV up by the same flat 5 percentage points and re-pricing the portfolio from there. The desk is heavily short Nifty puts across several strikes.
body.prompt: Why might this stress test understate the desk's real risk in an actual sharp selloff, and what should the risk manager change about it?
body.modelAnswer: A flat, parallel shock assumes every strike's IV rises by the same amount, which is closer to a mild sticky-delta-style shift than to how a genuine crash actually behaves. In a real sharp selloff, the skew itself tends to steepen: lower, put-side strikes rise in IV by more than the ATM or call-side strikes, as institutional hedging demand accelerates exactly when the feared move starts materializing. A book that is heavily short OTM puts is disproportionately hurt by that steepening, on top of the loss from spot falling and from the parallel level shift. The risk manager should add a non-parallel, skew-steepening component to the stress scenario, in addition to spot and level shocks, ideally calibrated to how skew actually moved during past sharp selloffs, rather than assuming the whole curve simply shifts up together.

body.text: Skew is not just something to read off a chart. It is a live map of where a book's risk actually concentrates, and that map redraws itself in a crash, usually against the exact positions that looked cheapest to run in calm markets. Trading and risk-managing options seriously means treating skew as a shape that moves, not a fixed cost to either harvest or ignore.

points: Selling rich, skew-driven OTM put premium is a real strategy, but the richness compensates for genuine crash risk; a calm-market track record does not test the risk it is actually short.

Put ratio spreads that sell extra further-OTM puts against a smaller long put position add uncovered downside exposure exactly where the skew is pricing real risk, a classic way "harvesting the skew" turns dangerous.

A risk reversal (sell OTM put, buy OTM call) is a tradeable structure, not just a sentiment metric; it expresses a directional view while remaining short some of the same tail risk skew-selling carries.
Sticky strike and sticky delta are the two standard conventions for how skew moves with spot; real markets often steepen further still during genuine selloffs, beyond either simple convention.
Flat, parallel IV stress tests understate risk for skew-heavy books; a more realistic stress test shocks the slope of the skew, not just its level, especially for positions short OTM puts.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The risk reversal trade example and the risk-manager scenario use rounded, illustrative figures, not live market data or a specific firm's actual risk model. Options strategies involving short volatility positions, including put selling and ratio spreads, carry substantial risk of large losses and are not suitable for every investor. Always check live prices and IV on NSE or your broker's terminal before trading, and consult a SEBI-registered advisor for personalised advice.
